Since the 1970s, scientists have been sending spacecraft to Mars. Over the years, various types of spacecraft have been launched, each designed for specific tasks. One type, known as orbiters, circles Mars and captures images as they travel around the planet. Another type, called landers, provides photos and data from their locations on the Martian surface. 
Rovers, which are equipped with wheels, specialize in mobility. They land on Mars and navigate to different areas, allowing scientists to explore the planet more thoroughly. Rovers play a crucial role in helping researchers understand the composition of various regions on Mars. The planet is made up of many types of rocks, and each rock consists of a mixture of chemicals. By moving around and studying these different rocks, rovers can analyze the unique chemical compositions found across the surface of Mars.

The Pioneer Venus project consisted of two spacecraft designed to explore the atmosphere and surface of Venus. Both spacecraft utilized a basic cylindrical bus design. Pioneer Venus 1 was the first of this orbiter-probe combination, specifically aimed at studying Venus's atmosphere. It became the first American spacecraft to orbit Venus.
Pioneer Venus 1 employed radar technology to map Venus's surface. The probe discovered that Venus is generally smoother than Earth, although it has a mountain higher than Mt. Everest and a chasm deeper than the Grand Canyon. Additionally, it confirmed that Venus has little to no magnetic field and found that the clouds primarily consist of sulfuric acid. The spacecraft eventually burned up in Venus's atmosphere, concluding a successful mission that lasted 14 years, far exceeding its original planned duration of eight months.
After a six-and-a-half-month journey, Pioneer Venus 1 entered an elliptical orbit around Venus at 15:58 UTC on December 4, 1978. This marked it as the first American spacecraft to enter orbit around Venus, occurring about three years after the Soviets achieved the same milestone.

What can you tell me about Venus?

Venus is the second planet from the Sun and the sixth largest planet in our solar system. It is the hottest planet, often referred to as Earth's twin due to its similar size. Venus is located approximately 38 million miles (about 61 million kilometers) from Earth. The planet features volcanic plains and rifts, and its thick atmosphere traps heat, contributing to its extreme temperatures. Although Venus is currently considered an unlikely place for life as we know it, it does lie within the Sun's "Goldilocks zone," which suggests that it may have been habitable in the past, potentially even before Earth.

What does JPL stand for, and what is it?

JPL stands for Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Is a federally funded research and development center managed for NASA by Caltech. It is a leader in robotic space exploration, sending rovers to Mars and probes to the farthest reaches of the solar system. The center also contributes to the construction of telescopes that observe some of the earliest galaxies, as well as satellites that enhance our understanding of Earth.

The Mars Rovers | NASA Space Place – NASA Science for Kids
Other spacecraft, called landers, provide photos and information from their landing spots on the surface of Mars.
Rovers have wheels and specialize in moving around. They land on the surface of Mars and drive around to different spots.
Rovers help scientists in their quest to understand what different parts of the planet are made of. Mars is made up of lots of different types of rocks, and each rock is made up of a mixture of chemicals. A rover can drive around to different areas, studying the different chemicals in each rock. These chemicals can tell scientists something about the environments that changed that rock over time.

Quick History

Mars has been known since ancient times because it can be seen without advanced telescopes.
There was even a flying helicopter on Mars. Seriously! The Mars Helicopter, Ingenuity, successfully tested powered, controlled flight on another world for the first time. It hitched a ride to Mars on the Perseverance rover and worked with the rover to explore Mars. Ingenuity was designed as a tech demo expected to fly no more than five times over 30 days. It ended its mission in early 2024 having completed 72 flights in just under three years. Thanks Ingenuity!
Several missions have orbited, landed on, or roved around on Mars: InSight, MAVEN, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, and many more! Mars is the only planet we have sent rovers to. They drive around Mars, taking pictures and measurements. Learn more about them and what they have discovered by clicking the pictures below!

Mars Rovers

Perseverance

Curiosity

Spirit and Opportunity

Sojourner

What does Mars look like?

Explore Mars! Click and drag to rotate the planet. Scroll or pinch to zoom in and out. Credit: NASA Visualization Technology Applications and Development (VTAD)

There are signs of ancient floods on Mars, but now water mostly exists in icy dirt and thin clouds. On some Martian hillsides, there is evidence of liquid salty water in the ground.
Scientists want to know if Mars may have had living things in the past. They also want to know if Mars could support life now or in the future.

Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

Structure and Surface

Mars is a terrestrial planet. It is small and rocky.
Mars has a thin atmosphere.
Mars has an active atmosphere, but the surface of the planet is not active. Its volcanoes are dead.

Time on Mars

One day on Mars lasts 24.6 hours. It is just a little longer than a day on Earth.
One year on Mars is 687 Earth days. It is almost twice as long as one year on Earth.

Mars’ Neighbors

Mars has two moons.
